subtitle: "A left hand that leaps: bass note, chord, bass note, chord"
---

[Open the Stride piano style in the Backing Track](../tools/backing-track.html?style=stride){.btn .btn-outline-primary}

## What it is

Solo piano music from Harlem in the late 1910s to the 1930s. The left hand does the work of a whole rhythm
section: a low bass note on beats 1 and 3 and a chord in the middle of the keyboard on 2 and 4, the hand
leaping ("striding") between them on every beat. The right hand plays the melody, decorated, over it.

Stride and [boogie-woogie](boogie.qmd) grew up side by side: both are piano music for dancing at parties,
both put a whole band into the left hand, and both feed into swing. They differ in what the left hand
does. The lesson [Two Left Hands](../lessons/stride-boogie.qmd) plays them side by side.

## A little history

Stride comes out of [ragtime](ragtime.qmd). A Scott Joplin rag already has the oom-pah left hand, written as a march.
In New York around the First World War, pianists such as James P. Johnson, Luckey Roberts and Willie
"The Lion" Smith played it faster and swung it, took it from rags to popular songs and the blues, and
added runs, tenths and cross-rhythms. They played at *rent parties*, where tenants paid the rent by
charging for food, drink and music, and in *cutting contests* against each other. Johnson's *Carolina
Shout* was the test piece: Duke Ellington learned it from a piano roll, slowed down.

Johnson's pupil Fats Waller made stride popular on records and radio, from 1934 with a small band,
*Fats Waller and His Rhythm*: bass, drums and guitar playing in two under the piano's left hand. That
is the sound this style copies. Art Tatum took stride to its technical limit; Count Basie began as a
stride pianist and pared it down to almost nothing; Thelonious Monk kept stride passages in his playing
all his life.

Johnson also wrote *Charleston* (1923). Its rhythm, a long note on 1 and a short one on the and of 2, is
the [Charleston comping figure](../lessons/patterns/chords-charleston.qmd) jazz pianists still use.

## The band's version

- **Comping:** *Stride*: on the piano, a low bass note on 1 and 3 (the root as an octave where a chord
  starts, its fifth on beat 3) and the chord in the middle of the keyboard on 2 and 4. On the guitar it
  is plain boom-chick.
- **Bass:** *Two-feel*: half notes on 1 and 3, with the piano's left hand.
- **Drums:** *Jazz time*, lightly.
- **Voicings:** plain triads and seventh chords, all their notes.

Real stride left hands reach for tenths, walk them up and down between chords, and break the pattern for
a run; the right hand carries the tune. The band's pianist keeps the pattern and plays no melody. That is
your part.

## Listening

| Recording | Year | Listen for |
|---|---|---|
| James P. Johnson, *Carolina Shout* | 1921 | The test piece of the Harlem pianists. |
| Fats Waller, *Handful of Keys* | 1929 | Stride at speed, solo. |
| Fats Waller, *Ain't Misbehavin'* (solo piano) | 1929 | The same left hand under a song. |
| Fats Waller and His Rhythm, *I'm Gonna Sit Right Down and Write Myself a Letter* | 1935 | Stride piano with bass and drums: this style. |
| Art Tatum, *Tiger Rag* | 1933 | Stride as virtuoso display. |
| Willie "The Lion" Smith, *Echoes of Spring* | 1939 | A gentler, more harmonic stride. |

## Sources

- Gunther Schuller, *Early Jazz* (Oxford, 1968), on James P. Johnson and the Harlem pianists.
- Willie "The Lion" Smith with George Hoefer, *Music on My Mind* (Doubleday, 1964), on rent parties and cutting contests.
- Scott E. Brown, *James P. Johnson: A Case of Mistaken Identity* (Scarecrow, 1986).
- Riccardo Scivales, *Jazz Piano: The Left Hand* (Ekay, 1990), on stride and boogie-woogie left hands.
